pharm: A magnesium salt of valproic acid that raises brain GABA and modulates sodium/calcium channels to suppress seizures and stabilize mood.
quick: Expressed as valproic acid equivalent; typically 600-2000 mg/day in divided doses, titrated
Take with or after food to reduce gastric upset
Contraindicated/avoid - highly teratogenic (neural tube defects, neurodevelopmental harm)
Excreted in milk in low amounts; generally considered compatible with monitoring
Dose adjustment may be needed; free fraction increases in uremia
Avoid; additive CNS depression and hepatic risk
Liver function, CBC/platelets, valproate levels, ammonia if symptomatic
summary: Magnesium valproate is a magnesium salt of valproic acid used as an antiepileptic and mood-stabilizing agent, available in some markets (e.g., India, Latin America) but not approved by the US FDA; doses are expressed in valproic acid equivalents. Like other valproates it raises GABA levels and modulates ion channels to control generalized and focal seizures and to treat bipolar mania. It carries the valproate class boxed risks of severe hepatotoxicity (especially in young children and mitochondrial disease), life-threatening pancreatitis, and major teratogenicity, including neural tube defects and impaired neurodevelopment.
indications: Generalized epilepsies (absence, myoclonic, tonic-clonic) and focal seizures
Bipolar disorder - treatment of manic episodes (where approved)

dosage.d: Valproate ~10-15 mg/kg/day (often ~600 mg/day) in divided doses
dosage.n: Doses expressed as valproic acid equivalent

dosage.d: Titrate to 1000-2000 mg/day (up to ~30-60 mg/kg/day) by clinical response and levels
Titrate per valproate guidance to therapeutic level and response

dosage.n: Avoid in children <2 years where possible (hepatotoxicity risk)

admin: Take with or after food to reduce gastrointestinal upset
Swallow whole if a modified-release form; do not crush unless the product allows
Titrate the dose gradually and adjust to response and plasma valproate levels
Do not stop abruptly in epilepsy (risk of status epilepticus); taper
moa: Valproate increases concentrations of the inhibitory neurotransmitter GABA in the brain (by stimulating its synthesis and inhibiting its degradation), and it blunts repetitive neuronal firing through effects on voltage-gated sodium channels and possibly T-type calcium channels. These combined actions raise the seizure threshold and reduce seizure spread, and contribute to its mood-stabilizing effect.

absolute: Hepatic disease or significant hepatic dysfunction; family history of severe valproate hepatotoxicity
Known mitochondrial disorders caused by POLG mutations (and suspected POLG disorders in children <2)
Pregnancy and women of childbearing potential not on a pregnancy-prevention program (per regulatory restrictions)
monitor: Liver function tests, especially in the first 6 months

preg: Valproate is a major human teratogen: it markedly increases the risk of neural tube defects, other congenital malformations, and impaired neurodevelopment (lower IQ, autism spectrum disorder). It is contraindicated in pregnancy unless no alternative exists, and women of childbearing potential must use effective contraception under a pregnancy-prevention program.
lact: Valproate is excreted into breast milk in low concentrations (about 1-10% of maternal plasma). Breastfeeding is generally considered compatible, but the infant should be monitored for sedation, poor feeding, and signs of hepatic or hematologic effects.
renal: In renal impairment the free (unbound) fraction of valproate rises because of reduced protein binding; total levels may mislead, so interpret free levels and adjust dose with caution.
hepatic: Valproate is hepatically metabolized and can cause severe hepatotoxicity; it is contraindicated in active hepatic disease or significant impairment.

major: Carbapenems (meropenem, etc.) - sharply lower valproate levels and seizure control; avoid
Lamotrigine - valproate raises lamotrigine levels and risk of serious rash; reduce lamotrigine dose
Other hepatotoxic drugs - additive liver injury
moderate: Enzyme-inducing antiepileptics (phenytoin, carbamazepine, phenobarbital) - reduce valproate levels
Aspirin/salicylates - displace valproate and increase free levels
interactions.food: Take with food to reduce gastric irritation.
interactions.alcohol: Avoid; additive CNS depression and hepatic toxicity.
interactions.diagnostics: May raise ammonia, cause thrombocytopenia, prolong bleeding time, and elevate transaminases.

monitoring: Liver function tests (baseline and periodic, especially first 6 months)
Pregnancy status in women of childbearing potential
counsel: Do not stop this medicine suddenly; stopping abruptly can cause seizures
Women: this drug can cause serious birth defects and developmental problems - use reliable contraception and tell your doctor before planning pregnancy
Report yellowing of skin/eyes, severe abdominal pain, persistent vomiting, unusual bruising/bleeding, or marked drowsiness/confusion
Take with food; expect possible weight gain, tremor, or hair thinning
Avoid alcohol and keep all blood-test appointments
pk: Anticonvulsant effect develops over days as levels stabilize
Supports 2-3 times daily dosing (less for modified release)
Store at 20-25 C (68-77 F); protect from heat and moisture
pearls: Not FDA-approved; marketed in some countries (e.g., India). This record is compiled from valproate/valproic acid class data and SmPC/BNF references; doses are valproic acid equivalents
Carries valproate class boxed risks: hepatotoxicity, pancreatitis, and teratogenicity
Carbapenems can abolish valproate levels - avoid the combination
Consider checking ammonia in any valproate patient with new confusion or lethargy
missed: Take the missed dose as soon as remembered; if it is almost time for the next dose, skip it. Do not double up. Do not stop without medical advice.
overdose: Overdose causes CNS depression ranging from drowsiness to coma, with miosis, respiratory depression, hypotension, metabolic disturbances, and sometimes hyperammonemia or cerebral edema. Treatment is supportive with airway/respiratory support; naloxone has been used (may reverse CNS depression but can also reverse anticonvulsant effect), and L-carnitine plus hemodialysis may help in severe poisoning.
